The Skinner Box. B.F. Skinner's operant conditioning chamber, which he developed from the 1930s onward, was a simple enclosed apparatus, but it shifted the entire direction of psychology. Inside, an animal—typically a rat or pigeon—learned to perform a behaviour, like pressing a lever, in order to receive reward or avoid punishment. Unlike Pavlov's classical conditioning, where the animal was passive, Skinner's box placed the animal at the center, actively learning through the consequences of its own actions.

A rat in the box discovers that pressing a lever dispenses food pellets. It learns to press repeatedly. This is reinforcement: positive reinforcement, when a reward follows behaviour, increases that behaviour's frequency. Negative reinforcement, when pressing the lever removes something unpleasant like an electric shock, also strengthens the behaviour. Punishment—adding something unpleasant after behaviour—weakens it. So does extinction, withdrawing the reward altogether.

What made Skinner's work particularly powerful was his discovery of schedules of reinforcement. Not every response needs to be rewarded. Skinner showed that a rat reinforced every fifth lever press behaves differently from a rat reinforced unpredictably, and both differ from a rat rewarded on a fixed time interval. Each schedule produces distinct patterns of behaviour, creating predictable results.

Skinner argued that these principles applied universally. The same mechanisms shaped rats, pigeons, humans, and complex behaviours. He went further, claiming that all behaviour—even language and moral conduct—is shaped by reinforcement history. His work demonstrated that behaviour could be precisely controlled and predicted through environmental manipulation alone.
